flows_intro.title: How Glasgow used its bike share
flows_intro.body: The data includes {summary.trips} trips between {summary.stations} nextbike stations, between September 2017 to April 2024. Weekdays carry about {weekday_per_day} trips a day with a morning and an evening commuting peak; weekend days carry {weekend_per_day}, spread across the afternoon. The station size varies depending on how many trips start or end there. Clicking a station reveals its top five origins and destinations. Through selecting in the legend you can compare weekdays with weekends. Pressing play under the map to shows the origin destination flow of a selected day type hour by hour.

Every station was described by the Census 2022 output areas within or touching a buffer around it, the study used a 250m buffer; (150m and 500m are shown for comparison). These are control variables in the regression model. The map colours the output areas themselves; click a station to draw its buffer, filled with the average of the buffer size selected.

infra_intro.title: Cycle infrastructure arrived while the system was running
infra_intro.body: The map shows Glasgow's cycle-route network. In the study I dated each segment that was opened during the data collection period. Dragging the slider or pressing play shows how the network grew over the collection period. The regression includes exposure to the network, so a route that gained a segregated lane part-way through the study changed exposure for every trip after that date.

corridors_intro.title: Finding commuter corridors
corridors_intro.body: The data included no trip purpose, so commuter corridors were found with k-means clustering (k = 2). Every station pair with more than 30 trips before COVID-19 (20 March 2020) was described by three features: peak share (share of weekday trips in the 07:00-10:00 and 16:00-19:00 peaks), the weekday : weekend ratio (logged) and reversal (does the main direction flip between morning and evening; 0 = never, 2 = completely). {n} of {summary.kmeans_pairs} pairs landed in the cluster with the higher value on all three, the commuter corridors. Switch metrics on and off to see the clusters from each angle; click a point, lasso a group or drag the range sliders to pick pairs and see their routes on the map. Pairs below the 30-trip threshold count as non-commuter in the regression.

regression_intro.title: Does cycle infrastructure attract bike-share trips?
regression_intro.body: A negative-binomial gravity model of trips between every pair of stations ({n_pairs} pairs, offset for the days both were live). Distance and the destination's workplace population behave as gravity predicts. Segregated infrastructure on its own has a small, uncertain effect, but on commuter corridors the effect is large: a commuter pair whose whole route is segregated is predicted to carry {irr_full}x the trips of one with none (95% CI {irr_lo} to {irr_hi}). At the median commuter exposure that is a {irr_median}x uplift. The map below shows the segregated segments and how many trips' routes followed them.

page.title: Glasgow Bike-Share Explorer
page.subtitle: Commuter-specific effects of segregated cycle infrastructure on bike-share use in Glasgow · MSc Urban Analytics, University of Glasgow
page.intro: Increasing active travel as a mode of transportation is a key policy goal of the Scottish  Government. Active travel provides health benefits to the population while reducing  dependence on private cars and the associated greenhouse gas emissions. Central to the aim  of increasing active travel use is the improvement of active travel infrastructure. My dissertation applied a negative binomial gravity model to 11,060 origin-destination pairs  derived from data of 1,202,020 trips taken using Glasgow’s nextbike bike sharing system.  Of the 11,060 origin-destination pairs 766 were identified as commuter corridors through k means clustering. Segregated lane infrastructure was found to be associated with a higher rate  of trips, an effect concentrated on commuter corridors (IRR 3.30 per unit of exposure) and  retained statistical significance under two-way Cameron, Gelbach, Miller clustering. The following maps and graphs display the data and the regression results, alongside the station-level variables used in the regression model.

headline.label: trip rate on a fully segregated commuter route

neighbourhoods.title: Surrounding Neighbourhood
neighbourhoods.body: The surrounding characteristics of each station influence its usage. The following three maps display the station-level variables included within the regression model.

notes.avg_age: the average age of residents within each buffer was calulcated using data from Scottish Census 2022 output areas.
notes.avg_health_score: average health was calculated using the Census self-reported health ratings these range from very bad (1) to very good (5); the buffer value is the mean response.
notes.avg_cars_per_household: the average number of cars or vans reported per household, ("four or more" was counted as four).
notes.cycling_distance_share_ext: share of commuters travelling 2 to 20 km to work. Under 2 km people were assumed to walk, and 20 km was taken as the furthest anyone would reasonably cycle to work.
notes.avg_nssec_score: the National Statistics Socio-economic Classification is scored from 1 (employers in large establishments) to 14 (never worked or long-term unemployed), with full-time students left out. The average score for each buffer zone was caculated - a lower average would suggest lower deprivation.
notes.student_share: full-time students as a share of the buffer's population. Studies have shown that students are a large proportion of bike-share users, so stations with a higher student share were expected to have more trips.
notes.over16pop: Residents aged 16+ count at both ends of a trip: someone who rides to work in the morning usually rides home to the station nearest where they live in the evening.
notes.workplace_pop: Workplace population (people who work in the buffer, wherever they live) counts only at the destination: the weekday morning peak pulls commuters into job-rich stations, but they disperse before heading home in the evening.
notes.n_on_premises: Premises licensed for alcohol to be drunk on site stand in for the night-time economy: concerts, theatres, sports and nights out. The count within the buffer entered the model at the destination only, since people may cycle out for the evening but are less likely to cycle home.
notes.premises_capacity: the summed licensed capacity of those premises.
